A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the SHARE dataset and EPISODE framework. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained and revised content.

before.justification: V1 reports original dialogue-generation evaluations in Tables 3–5, information-extraction results in Table 6, and human-evaluation results in Table 7.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds individual-memory and prior-method comparison results in Tables 3–4, plus dataset genre counts in Figure 5.

M1.justification: EPISODE retains the same memory selection, response generation, information extraction, and four memory-update operations. The appendix prompts are identical. Newly documented LoRA settings and experimental model labels do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same English movie-dialogue dataset, reporting 1,201 scripts, 3,216 episodes, and 17,679 sessions. Figure 5 describes the existing genre mixture; it does not establish added domains or tasks. The new memory comparisons retain the existing dialogue tasks.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds predicted individual memory for both backbones. Table 4 adds COMEDY and LLM-Rsum alongside the retained comparisons. This substantially broadens the main evaluation from internal memory variants to established long-term dialogue methods; their earlier citations alone did not constitute evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 reports Llama-3.1-Instruct instead of Llama-3-Instruct in Section 5.1 and Tables 3–4, and GPT-4o instead of GPT-4 as evaluator. These are reported setting revisions, without evidence establishing reruns; Table 5 still names Llama-3. V2 also describes consistency as an unchanged relationship, whereas the unchanged Table 21 prompt allows justified relationship evolution.

E4.justification: The new individual-memory control in Table 3 tests independently managed speaker memories and the contribution of the interlocutor's persona and personal-event information. This extends the existing memory ablations. The information-extraction analysis, human study, and substantive Figure 3 case study are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.6 retains five evaluations per criterion with averaged results. Appendix A.7 retains seed 2025, 25 sampled conversations, and 20 annotators per conversation. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or additional uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 3–4 substantially expand comparative results through the new baselines. EPISODE generally performs better, although Llama-based LLM-Rsum has higher coherence in sessions 5–6. The accumulation row's session-6 Llama coherence changes from 2.6583 to 2.5958 under revised setting labels. Figure 5 adds genre counts; Tables 5–7 retain their numerical results.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 adds an explicit task assumption that both participants can access and use all memory types extracted from their conversations. The mathematical task definitions and response mappings remain unchanged, and neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain SHARE, EPISODE, and evidence that shared memories improve long-term dialogue quality. The conclusion now highlights GPT-Eval, which was already used and cited in v1. The added comparisons support the retained contributions rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting individual-memory results to interlocutor information and attributing LLM-Rsum's weaknesses to compressed memory units. It discusses applicability to varied dialogue styles and adds a limitation about inconsistencies from mixing GPT models. The earlier budget-related qualification of the human evaluation is removed without an expanded study.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents episode-level 8:1:1 partitioning, session counts of 14,255/1,739/1,685 for training/validation/testing, LoRA rank 16, and annotator eligibility. It replaces the anonymous dataset-only link with advertised dataset-and-code access. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation, although v1's explicit GPT-4o attribution for memory-selector training-data generation is removed.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to Akoury et al. on game dialogue, Chen et al. on Harry Potter dialogue agents, and Hu et al. on LoRA. Already-cited COMEDY and recursive summarization receive direct comparative positioning. The related-work sections and central novelty positioning otherwise remain stable.

P1.justification: V2 revises selected introduction, method, results, case-study, and conclusion passages, condenses metric descriptions, and updates affiliations, contribution notes, and acknowledgments. These primarily clarify or shorten existing explanations while retaining the section sequence and overall narrative.

P2.justification: Tables 3–4 expand to accommodate new comparator rows, and Figure 5 adds a genre-distribution chart. Figures 2–3 are reformatted while retaining their substantive illustrations; Figure 3 moves and standardizes a speaker name. Appendix Tables 8–23 and the human-evaluation interface are visually unchanged.

improvement.justification: The added prior-method baselines and individual-memory control strengthen evidence beyond v1's mainly internal comparisons. Data-split, LoRA, annotator, and code-access disclosures also improve reproducibility. These benefits support a limited net improvement, tempered by inconsistent Llama labels, unexplained evaluator relabeling alongside largely retained scores, and a revised consistency description that conflicts with the unchanged Table 21 prompt.
